findings.title: IAM policy allows all actions on all resources
findings.description: An Allow statement with Action "*" on Resource "*" is administrative access. Scope actions and resources to least privilege.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statement with Action "*" on Resource "*"

findings.title: RDS instance without deletion protection
findings.description: Deletion protection guards against accidental database destruction. The provider default is false.

findings.title: RDS instance publicly accessible
findings.description: A publicly accessible database accepts connections from the internet. Keep databases in private subnets with publicly_accessible false (the provider default).
findings.remediation:
Set `publicly_accessible = false` and move the database to private subnets:
resource "aws_db_instance" "this" {
  # ...
  publicly_accessible = false
  db_subnet_group_name = aws_db_subnet_group.private.name
}
Access the database via a bastion host, VPN, or SSM port forwarding — never directly.

findings.title: IAM managed policy grants administrative access
findings.description: An Allow statement with Action "*" (or "iam:*") on Resource "*" is administrative access in a customer-managed policy. Scope actions and resources to least privilege.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statement with Action "*"/"iam:*" on Resource "*"
findings.remediation:
Replace the admin-managed policy attachment with scoped inline or customer-managed
policies (see AEGIS-AWS-006 fix). If break-glass admin access is required, gate it
behind a separate role with MFA condition and CloudTrail alerting:
Condition = { Bool = { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent" = "true" } }

path.detail: any identity attached to this policy gains administrative access

findings.title: RDS without IAM database authentication
findings.description: With iam_database_authentication_enabled absent or false, database access relies on long-lived passwords instead of short-lived IAM credentials, weakening credential hygiene.

findings.title: Hardcoded credentials in resource config
findings.description: A database password written as a literal in Terraform config is stored in state, plan output, and version control. The same holds for a secret-like variable or local flowing into a credential attribute. Reference a secrets manager or a generated password instead. The secret value is never included in findings.
findings.expected: reference to a secrets manager or generated password
findings.remediation:
Remove the hardcoded credential and rotate it immediately — it is compromised.
Reference a Secrets Manager secret instead:
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = aws_secretsmanager_secret.db.id
}
# then: password = jsondecode(data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db.secret_string)["password"]
If the value was committed to git, purge it from history (BFG/truffleHog) and rotate.

findings.title: RDS instance without Multi-AZ
findings.description: Single-AZ RDS instances have no standby for failover. Enable multi_az for production databases.

findings.title: IAM policy allows privilege escalation (create policy + attach policy)
findings.description: The policy combines a policy-authoring action (iam:CreatePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:PutGroupPolicy) with a policy-attachment action (iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:AttachGroupPolicy). Attack path: create an administrative policy, attach it to your own role/user, assume full admin. Split authoring from attachment duties and scope each to least privilege.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statements grant policy-authoring and policy-attachment actions
findings.expected: separate policy authoring from attachment; scope both to least privilege
findings.remediation:
Split policy authoring from attachment (this combination is the classic privilege
escalation primitive). Remove `iam:CreatePolicy*` / `iam:Attach*Policy` from the
workload policy. Policy management belongs in a separate, human-gated CI/CD role —
never in an application runtime role.

findings.title: IAM policy allows privilege escalation via iam:PassRole on * with compute launch
findings.description: The policy allows iam:PassRole on "*" together with a role-assumption primitive (ec2:RunInstances, lambda:CreateFunction, lambda:UpdateFunctionCode, ...). Attack path: launch a compute resource passing an administrative role, then steal its credentials from the instance metadata / environment. Scope iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statements grant iam:PassRole on "*" with a compute-launch primitive
findings.expected: scope iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs
findings.remediation:
Scope `iam:PassRole` to the exact role ARNs the workload must pass, and only
together with the specific compute-launch action it needs:
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "iam:PassRole",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AppExecutionRole"
}
Never grant `iam:PassRole` on `*` — it lets the holder escalate to any role.

findings.title: IAM policy allows data exfiltration primitives
findings.description: The policy grants a known exfiltration pair: s3:GetObject + s3:PutObject on "*" (copy data to an attacker bucket), rds:CreateDBSnapshot + rds:ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute (share a snapshot cross-account), or ec2:CreateSnapshot + ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute (share an EBS snapshot). Attack path: snapshot or copy production data, share it outside the account. Scope data-plane actions to specific resources.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statements grant exfiltration pair s3:GetObject + s3:PutObject on "*"
findings.expected: scope data-plane actions to specific resources
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: IAM permissions management actions allowed on all resources
findings.description: An Allow statement grants IAM write actions (iam:Put*, iam:Create*, iam:Update*, iam:Delete*, iam:Attach*, iam:Detach*, or iam:*) on Resource "*". Attack path: modify any identity's policies directly to escalate to admin. Read-only IAM actions (iam:Get*, iam:List*, iam:Generate*, iam:Simulate*) are excluded. Scope IAM management to specific users, roles, and policies.
findings.evidence: policy = Allow statement grants IAM management action "*" on "*"
findings.expected: scope IAM management actions to specific identities
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: RDS MySQL/Postgres instance without IAM database authentication
findings.description: MySQL and Postgres RDS instances support IAM database authentication, which replaces long-lived passwords with short-lived IAM credentials. With iam_database_authentication_enabled absent or false, access relies on static passwords. Engine-scoped: only fires for mysql/postgres engines; aurora and unknown engines are out of scope.

findings.title: RDS instance without CloudWatch log exports
findings.description: Hygiene: RDS instances should export database logs to CloudWatch via enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports for auditing and troubleshooting. Without log exports, forensic analysis after an incident is limited.
findings.remediation: Enable audit logging. Turn on CloudTrail (multi-region, log file validation, KMS-encrypted bucket), VPC flow logs, and service access logs. Ship logs to a dedicated, MFA-delete-protected bucket in a security account.

findings.title: RDS instance without copy_tags_to_snapshot
findings.description: Hygiene: RDS instances should copy tags to snapshots so backup resources inherit cost-allocation and ownership tags. Set copy_tags_to_snapshot = true.

findings.title: RDS instance without enhanced monitoring
findings.description: Hygiene: RDS instances should enable enhanced monitoring (monitoring_interval > 0) for OS-level metrics that aid troubleshooting. Set monitoring_interval to 1, 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60.
findings.remediation:
Enable Enhanced Monitoring on the RDS instance (1-second OS metrics):
resource "aws_db_instance" "this" {
  # ...
  monitoring_interval = 60
  monitoring_role_arn = aws_iam_role.rds_enhanced_monitoring.arn
}
monitoring_interval accepts 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, or 60 (seconds); any
non-zero value requires a monitoring_role_arn with the
rds-monitoring-role trust policy.

findings.title: RDS Postgres instance without query logging
findings.description: Hygiene: RDS Postgres instances should export postgresql logs to CloudWatch for query auditing. Add "postgresql" to enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports.
findings.remediation: Enable audit logging. Turn on CloudTrail (multi-region, log file validation, KMS-encrypted bucket), VPC flow logs, and service access logs. Ship logs to a dedicated, MFA-delete-protected bucket in a security account.

findings.title: RDS instance without Performance Insights
findings.description: Hygiene: RDS instances should enable Performance Insights for query-level performance analysis. Set performance_insights_enabled = true.
findings.remediation: Review the flagged configuration against AWS security best practices and the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Apply the control the rule describes, preferring restrictive defaults, encryption, and audit logging. Validate with `aegis scan` after the change.

findings.title: IAM user has no tags
findings.description: The IAM user carries no tags, making ownership, purpose, and lifecycle untraceable in audits and complicating attribute-based access control. Tag identities with at least owner and purpose.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: IAM policy statement has no Sid
findings.description: At least one policy statement has no Sid, making the statement harder to reference in reviews, audit findings, and exception tracking. Give every statement a descriptive Sid.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: RDS instance on the default option group
findings.description: option_group_name is absent or a default group, so the instance runs with AWS's generic options (e.g. no OEM, no MariaDB audit plugin). Use a purpose-built option group.
findings.evidence: option_group_name = absent (provider default: default option group)
findings.remediation: Review the flagged configuration against AWS security best practices and the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Apply the control the rule describes, preferring restrictive defaults, encryption, and audit logging. Validate with `aegis scan` after the change.

findings.title: RDS master password not managed by Secrets Manager
findings.description: A plaintext master password is set without manage_master_user_password, so the credential sits in state and is never rotated automatically. Use manage_master_user_password = true so RDS manages rotation in Secrets Manager. The password value is never included in findings.
findings.remediation: Remove the hardcoded secret immediately and rotate it. Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store (SecureString) and reference them via data sources. Never commit secrets to version control — scan history with gitleaks if the value was ever committed.
